title: Towards Standardized Evaluation of GPU Memory Safety with GMSBench

numericClaims.quote: GMSBench comprises 149 self-contained CUDA tests covering spatial errors, temporal errors, and data races across various GPU memory spaces and object relationships, as summarized in Figure 1.

we evaluate the suite on three NVIDIA GPU platforms: a workstation-grade RTX A5000 (Ampere, SM_86) and a datacenter A100 (Ampere, SM_80), both with x86 hosts, and a datacenter GH200 Grace Hopper system with an AArch64 Grace CPU and Hopper GPU (SM_90).
Memcheck, CompSan’s memory-error detection tool, detected only 18/144 tests across the spatial and temporal error classes.
racecheck detects 2/5 race tests, correctly identifying both shared-memory races while missing all three global-memory races.
cuCatch [4] used a set of 56 CUDA tests covering spatial and temporal violations across global, local, and shared memory but is not publicly available and uses a relatively coarse classification.

CuSafe [5] provides an open-source benchmark containing 33 tests covering spatial and temporal errors, including linear and non-linear overflows and local memory violations, but remains limited in size and taxonomy.

questions.question: How many tests does GMSBench comprise and which error classes do they span?
questions.answer: 149 self-contained CUDA tests spanning spatial errors, temporal errors, and data races (concurrency errors) across various GPU memory spaces and object relationships.

questions.question: Which tool does GMSBench evaluate, and with which sub-tools or variants?
questions.answer: NVIDIA Compute Sanitizer (CompSan), using its memcheck, initcheck, and racecheck tools, plus a variant of memcheck with API errors enabled called apicheck (memcheck with --report-api-errors=explicit).

questions.question: On which GPU platforms is the benchmark evaluated, and what cross-platform behavior is observed?
questions.answer: Three NVIDIA platforms: a workstation-grade RTX A5000 (Ampere, SM_86) and a datacenter A100 (Ampere, SM_80), both with x86 hosts, and a GH200 Grace Hopper system with an AArch64 Grace CPU and Hopper GPU (SM_90). Native manifestation and tool verdicts are identical across all three architectures, even for local-memory tests and data races.

questions.question: What are GMSBench's four design principles?
questions.answer: Systematic Coverage, Violation Isolation (each self-contained test isolates a single violation), Independent Ground Truth (baseline native execution without protection), and Mechanism-Agnostic design (tests independent of any particular detection mechanism, with a shared harness).

questions.question: What four dimensions does the GMSBench taxonomy use to classify tests?
questions.answer: (1) Error class (spatial, temporal, or data race); (2) Memory window (global, local, shared, constant, including cross-space accesses); (3) Object context (allocation mechanism and object relationships, e.g., static/dynamic, intra-/inter-object, adjacency); (4) Violation type (linear over-reads/writes, targeted OOB read/write, use-after-free, invalid free, double free, uninitialized read, use-after-scope, use-after-return, lost update).

questions.question: How does GMSBench establish ground truth, and how are tests without reliable native manifestation handled?
questions.answer: Through baseline execution that runs each test natively on the GPU without any protection mechanism, checking for observable effects: sentinel corruption for write violations, disclosure of a planted value for OOB reads, deterministic incorrect results for data races, and the CUDA runtime's rejection of illegal deallocations for invalid/double frees. Tests without reliable native manifestation are marked as detection-only and evaluated using the mechanism's own diagnostic output.

questions.question: What fraction of tests manifest natively, and how many spatial/temporal tests does memcheck detect?
questions.answer: 134/149 tests (90%) manifest during native CUDA execution; memcheck detects only 18/144 applicable spatial and temporal tests (12.5%).

questions.question: Which memcheck detection gaps does the evaluation reveal, and what is the device-heap exception?
questions.answer: Because memcheck is tripwire-based, it misses linear overflows that land directly in another live allocation (adjacent buffers or buffers separated by a live intervening object) and targeted OOB accesses that jump over the tripwire; it also misses all intra-object and cross-space violations (no sub-object bounds or pointer-provenance tracking) and delayed/aliased UAFs (no allocation-identity tracking after address reuse). The exception is device-heap memory from in-kernel malloc(), where memcheck detects all linear overflow variants, including accesses into live neighboring objects.

questions.question: How do apicheck, initcheck, and racecheck perform within their intended scopes?
questions.answer: apicheck detects 10/11 invalid- and double-free tests by reporting CUDA API errors but misses the device-heap double free performed through in-kernel free(); initcheck detects all 4/4 uninitialized-read tests; racecheck detects 2/5 race tests, correctly identifying both shared-memory races while missing all three global-memory races.

questions.question: How do the prior benchmarks cuCatch and CuSafe compare to GMSBench?
questions.answer: cuCatch used 56 CUDA tests covering spatial and temporal violations across global, local, and shared memory but is not publicly available and uses a coarse classification; CuSafe provides an open-source benchmark of 33 tests covering spatial and temporal errors but is limited in size and taxonomy. Neither systematically covers constant memory, host-pinned memory, cross-window provenance violations, uninitialized reads, aliased UAF, or data races under a single taxonomy, whereas GMSBench offers 149 open-source tests with a finer-grained taxonomy.

questions.question: Why are use-after-free, invalid free, and double free not covered for shared memory?
questions.answer: Because shared memory is scoped to a thread block and has no explicit object deallocation during kernel execution; additionally, a reliable ground truth could not be established for shared-memory uninitialized reads.

questions.question: Why does cudaMallocManaged() contribute no spatial tests to GMSBench?
questions.answer: Because its tested behavior was equivalent to cudaMalloc() (footnote 2); managed memory instead contributes a delayed UAF variant in the temporal class.

questions.question: What runtime overhead does Compute Sanitizer's memcheck incur when running the GMSBench tests?
How many OpenCL tests are included in GMSBench?
What detection rate does cuCatch achieve on GMSBench's cross-space violation tests?
